questions.subtopic: 4A5 Confidentiality and proper use of information. Personal use without disclosure
questions.question: Internal auditor Sina quotes a design firm's senior pay range, seen in payroll workpapers, without names, when asking the human resources head, who sets those ranges, for a raise. Which assessment is MOST accurate?

options.A: It is misuse, since engagement information served a personal gain
options.B: It is proper, since nothing reached an unauthorized party
options.C: It is proper, since nobody was identified or put at a loss
options.D: It is misuse, since pay data was disclosed without authorization

questions.key_concept: Using engagement information for personal gain is misuse in itself, even when nothing is disclosed to an unauthorized party and nobody is harmed.
questions.pre_read: Separate two questions: who learned the information, and what was it used for?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 5.1 Use of Information bars internal auditors from using information for personal gain, and that test is about use, not about who else learns it or who loses. Sina took the pay range from engagement workpapers to strengthen a personal pay claim, so it is misuse although human resources already knew the figures. That nothing was disclosed is the runner-up: correct under Standard 5.2 Protection of Information, but disclosure is a separate rule.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: no unauthorized party learned anything, so the disclosure rule is not broken. The separate rule against using information for personal gain is.
wrong_explanations.C: Harm and naming matter when judging a privacy exposure. The bar on personal gain does not depend on anyone losing or being identified.
wrong_explanations.D: The human resources head sets the ranges and is entitled to the figures, so nothing was disclosed without authorization. The fault lies in what Sina used them for.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the bar on personal gain needs no victim, and D, because the human resources head is entitled to pay data, so nothing was disclosed without authorization.
Final two: A beats B because use and disclosure are separate rules: nothing was disclosed, yet engagement information still served Sina's own benefit.
Exam cue: test information questions twice. Was it disclosed to someone unauthorized? Was it used for anything but the work? Either one is enough.

questions.subtopic: 4A2 Threats to internal audit independence. A governing structure that limits independence
questions.question: A Paraguayan farm cooperative's members elect a board of its department heads, whose areas internal audit reviews; chief audit executive Sofía reports to that board. What is MOST clearly required of Sofía?

options.A: Record the reasons a condition is agreed unnecessary, and its substitute
options.B: Document how the structure limits independence, and possible safeguards
options.C: Tell the board that the function cannot conform with the Standards
options.D: Arrange independent outside assurance over the areas board members manage

questions.key_concept: When the governing structure itself does not support independence, the chief audit executive must document what limits it and the safeguards that could be used.
questions.pre_read: Several documenting duties exist for gaps in governance. Which one fits a structure that cannot support independence?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 7.1 sets a duty for this case: when the governing structure cannot support the function's independence, the chief audit executive must record what in it limits independence and which safeguards could help. A board of the managers whose areas internal audit reviews is such a structure. Concluding the function cannot conform, the closest choice, is a step the Domain III introduction allows, not requires, when the reasons for an unmet essential condition are disputed.

wrong_explanations.A: That record is required when the chief audit executive, the board and senior management agree an essential condition is unnecessary. No such agreement is described here.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: Domain III allows, not requires, that conclusion when the reasons for an unmet essential condition are disputed. Standard 7.1's documented limits and safeguards answer this structure.
wrong_explanations.D: Alternative assurance is required over areas internal audit would review that the chief audit executive runs beyond internal auditing. Here the issue is the board's makeup.

tips: Eliminate: A, because that record follows an agreement that an essential condition is unnecessary, and D, because alternative assurance is for areas the chief audit executive is responsible for beyond internal auditing.
Final two: B beats C because Standard 7.1 requires documenting the structure's limits and possible safeguards, while concluding nonconformance is an option tied to disputed essential conditions.

Exam cue: match each documenting duty to its trigger. A structure limiting independence: its limits and safeguards (must). An agreed unneeded condition: reasons and substitutes (must). A disputed one: why it is refused (should).

questions.subtopic: 4A2 Threats to internal audit independence. After a session without senior management
questions.question: After a private session with a Malawian tea estate's audit committee on staffing gaps and next year's coverage, the chief executive asks chief audit executive Chikondi what was discussed. What is Chikondi's BEST response?

options.A: Decline, as sessions without senior management are kept from it
options.B: Decline, and note the request in the yearly independence confirmation
options.C: Brief the chief executive, whose approval the coverage changes need
options.D: Brief the chief executive on the resourcing and coverage points

questions.key_concept: A private board session protects a channel, not a secret: senior management should hear what was discussed, unless it concerns, say, a senior manager's misconduct.
questions.pre_read: Private sessions protect the chief audit executive's access to the board. Does that make everything said there secret from senior management?
questions.correct_explanation: Private sessions give the chief audit executive a channel to the board, not a duty of secrecy. Standard 9.4 requires the plan and the effect of resource limits on coverage to be shared with senior management, and Standard 6.3 requires board communications to be coordinated with it; its considerations add that private talks are passed on unless the subject is, say, a senior manager's misconduct. Declining, the closest choice, fits only that case.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: withholding fits a private session about a senior manager's own conduct. Staffing gaps and coverage are matters Standard 9.4 requires sharing with senior management anyway.
wrong_explanations.B: The yearly confirmation reports incidents that may have impaired independence. A chief executive asking about routine matters is not interference.
wrong_explanations.C: The board approves the internal audit plan and significant changes to it. Senior management gives input on coverage; it does not approve it.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a question about routine matters is not an incident that impairs independence, and C, because the board approves coverage changes, with senior management giving input.

Final two: D beats A because private sessions keep the board channel open without a duty of secrecy; withholding fits only a subject like a senior manager's misconduct, and coverage must be shared anyway.
Exam cue: private sessions keep a channel to the board open; they do not shut senior management out. Ask what the session was about before deciding who may hear of it.

questions.subtopic: 4A2 Threats to internal audit independence. A reporting line to the board on paper only
questions.question: A Qatari shipper's charter has chief audit executive Hamad report to the audit committee, but the chief executive edits and presents Hamad's reports at meetings Hamad never attends. Which assessment is MOST accurate?

options.A: Impaired independence: management stands between Hamad and the board
options.B: No impairment: reporting through the chief executive is leading practice
options.C: Impaired objectivity: Hamad must disclose it to the board
options.D: A scope limitation: Hamad discusses it, then elevates it to the board

questions.key_concept: A functional line to the board that exists only on paper does not support independence. The chief audit executive needs direct communication with the board.
questions.pre_read: A reporting line can be written into the charter and still not work. What makes a functional line to the board real?
questions.correct_explanation: Principle 7 and Standard 7.1 rest independence on the chief audit executive reporting directly to the board, and the considerations list a chief audit executive without direct communication or interaction with the board as a situation that may impair it. Here the chief executive filters and presents Hamad's reports, so the charter's line does not work. Calling it leading practice, the closest choice, confuses it with the administrative line, which the chief executive may hold.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: an administrative line to the chief executive is leading practice. The functional line must still run directly to the board, and here it does not.
wrong_explanations.C: Objectivity is each auditor's unbiased mindset. The problem here is the function's position, a matter of independence, not Hamad's personal judgment.
wrong_explanations.D: A scope limitation is a condition inside an engagement, such as restricted access to records. This is a defect in the function's reporting line.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the problem lies in the function's position, not in Hamad's own mindset, and D, because scope limitations are conditions inside an engagement, not a reporting-line defect.
Final two: A beats B because the chief executive may hold the administrative line, but the functional line must reach the board directly, without management editing what the board receives.

Exam cue: judge the line by what happens, not by the charter. If management edits internal audit's reports or stands between the chief audit executive and the board, the functional line is not working.

questions.subtopic: 4A3 Internal audit and the Three Lines Model. Where a support department sits
questions.question: At an Omani hospital group, internal auditor Salim must place the HR department, which reports to the chief operating officer and runs hiring and payroll. Under current IIA Three Lines guidance, which placement is BEST?

options.A: Second line: it serves every hospital in the group as shared support
options.B: First line: it reports to a member of senior management
options.C: First line: back-office work is part of running the organization
options.D: Second line: it is organizationally separate from the wards

questions.key_concept: Three Lines: work that runs the organization, back office included, is first line; the second line gives specialist support and challenge on risk.
questions.pre_read: Support departments serve the whole organization. Does that make them second line, or part of running the business?
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's 2026 statement on the Three Lines Model counts all work that runs the organization as first line, in back offices as much as on the front line, and keeps the second line for specialist roles that support and challenge on risk. Its notes say some organizations call support departments second line; the model does not. HR's hiring and payroll run operations. Serving every hospital, the closest choice, does not change that.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: some organizations do call support departments second line. The 2026 statement puts back-office work in the first line and keeps the second for specialist roles on risk.
wrong_explanations.B: First line is right, but not for that reason. Second-line roles also report to members of senior management, so the reporting line does not decide the placement.
wrong_explanations.D: Separation from operations is a strength of second-line roles, but it does not make a department one. HR's own work is running processes, which is first line.

tips: Eliminate: B, because second-line roles also report to senior managers, so that reason cannot place HR, and D, because separation from the wards does not turn operational work into second-line work.
Final two: C beats A because the 2026 statement places back-office work in the first line; serving many units does not make a department a risk-focused specialist.
Exam cue: place a role by what it does. Running a process is first line; specialist support, monitoring and challenge on risk is second line; independent assurance is third.

questions.subtopic: 4A4 Objectivity impairments of individual auditors. Fixed ideas about a group of people
questions.question: Internal auditor Mattias, new to an Austrian bakery chain, calls identical missing sign-offs oversights at one branch and carelessness at the branch staffed mainly by workers from abroad. Which threat to objectivity is MOST evident?

options.A: Prejudice or unconscious bias, from fixed ideas about a group
options.B: Familiarity bias, from assumptions carried over from past experience
options.C: Self-review bias, from judging work that Mattias helped to shape
options.D: A conflict of interest, from a personal stake in one branch's result

questions.key_concept: The Standards' examples of bias include self-review, familiarity, and prejudice or unconscious bias: fixed ideas about a group distorting how information is read.
questions.pre_read: Where does the different reading come from: Mattias's history with these branches, Mattias's own earlier work, a personal stake, or the people involved?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 2.1 Individual Objectivity requires internal auditors to know and manage their biases, and its considerations name prejudice or unconscious bias: preconceptions about a group of people that skew how evidence is read. Mattias treats identical gaps differently, and the one variable is who works at each branch. Familiarity bias, the runner-up, is assumptions carried from past experience; the stem shows no such experience at work here.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: familiarity bias lets assumptions from past experience replace evidence. Nothing in the stem shows such experience; the one variable between the branches is their staff.
wrong_explanations.C: Self-review bias arises when auditors assess work they designed or performed. Nothing in the stem shows Mattias had any hand in either branch's sign-off process.
wrong_explanations.D: A conflict of interest needs a competing personal interest, such as a relative at a branch or a financial tie. The stem gives Mattias none.

tips: Eliminate: C, because Mattias had no hand in either branch's work, and D, because no relative, money or other personal interest ties Mattias to a branch.
Final two: A beats B because familiarity bias carries assumptions from past experience, while here identical evidence is read differently and the only variable is who the staff are.
Exam cue: when identical evidence gets different treatment and the only difference is the people involved, think prejudice or unconscious bias, not familiarity or self-review.

questions.subtopic: 4A4 Objectivity impairments of individual auditors. A bonus for each significant finding
questions.question: To reward rigor, the chief audit executive of a Panamanian shipping agent proposes a bonus for each significant finding an internal auditor reports, with no input from audited managers. Which view is MOST accurate?

options.A: Sound: it rewards skepticism, which guards auditors' judgments against bias
options.B: Sound: audited managers have no say in the auditors' pay
options.C: Unsound: it rewards findings that management has not yet accepted
options.D: Unsound: paying per finding gives auditors a stake in the results

questions.key_concept: Pay designs can impair objectivity: a bonus per finding gives auditors a personal stake in finding problems, as ratings from audited managers reward finding none.
questions.pre_read: Read each view's reason, not just its verdict. Does the reason match what the scheme actually rewards?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity requires auditors to avoid conflicts of interest, and its considerations say the chief audit executive should guard against pay designs that may impair objectivity, naming performance judged on how many findings auditors raise. A bonus per finding gives each auditor a stake in reporting problems. Keeping audited managers out of pay, the runner-up, removes one bias but leaves this one.

wrong_explanations.A: Skepticism concerns how information is judged, not how many findings result. Paying per finding rewards a count, which can tilt judgment toward reporting problems.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: pay resting mainly on audited managers' views is a named risk, and this scheme avoids it. Rewarding the number of findings is a separate risk to objectivity.
wrong_explanations.C: Findings do not need management's acceptance to stand; auditors need not change results without a valid reason. The scheme's flaw is the stake in the count.

tips: Eliminate: A, because skepticism is about judging information, not producing more findings, and C, because a finding does not need management's acceptance to stand.
Final two: D beats B because bias can run either way: removing audited managers' input ends one pull, while paying per finding adds a pull toward reporting problems.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, a reward that depends on what engagements conclude, more findings or happier managers, can impair objectivity even when audited managers have no say.

questions.subtopic: 4A5 Confidentiality and proper use of information. Confidential data for a guest auditor
questions.question: Guest auditor Tine, seconded from a Slovenian insurer's IT team under internal audit's confidentiality rules, will match sales executives' named pay rises to committee minutes. What is engagement supervisor Mira's BEST course?

options.A: Give Tine masked records, since executives' names are personal information
options.B: Keep the pay data from Tine, who is not internal audit staff
options.C: Let the payroll head decide what Tine sees, as the data's owner
options.D: Give Tine the named pay records that the matching test requires

questions.key_concept: Authorization follows the work: people assisting internal audit may use the confidential data the work needs, held to the same protection rules as its staff.
questions.pre_read: Is Tine authorized for this data because of the engagement, and what does the test actually need to see?
questions.correct_explanation: Principle 5 Maintain Confidentiality limits information to professional use and guards it against people without authorization, and Standard 5.2 requires the chief audit executive to hold everyone assisting the function to the same protection rules. Tine assists the engagement under those rules, and matching pay rises to minutes needs names. Masked records, the runner-up, would hide the very detail the test needs.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: masking suits tests that do not need identities. Matching named executives' rises to committee minutes does, and Tine is authorized for the work.
wrong_explanations.B: Authorization comes from the work, not from which department someone belongs to. Standard 5.2 expects people assisting the function to follow the same protection rules, not to be shut out.
wrong_explanations.C: The payroll head owns the data but does not decide what internal audit needs for its work; unrestricted access is part of the mandate. Restricting it would limit the scope.

tips: Eliminate: B, because authorization follows the work, not the department Tine comes from, and C, because the data's owner does not decide what an engagement may see.
Final two: D beats A because the test cannot match minutes without names; protection comes from holding Tine to the function's rules, not from hiding what the work needs.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, confidentiality limits who may see data and why; someone assisting an engagement under the function's rules is authorized for what the work requires.

questions.subtopic: 4A5 Confidentiality and proper use of information. A personal detail the work does not need
questions.question: Interviewing a Rwandan exporter's warehouse manager, internal auditor Uwase hears of a colleague's medical treatment, unrelated to the audit; privacy policy limits health data to tasks needing it. What is Uwase's BEST course?

options.A: Record it, since workpapers must let a reviewer redo the work
options.B: Leave it out of the interview notes kept in the workpapers
options.C: Record it, and mark that workpaper confidential with restricted access
options.D: Report it to human resources, which handles staff health matters

questions.key_concept: Information is collected and kept as policy allows: personal health details the work does not need stay out of the workpapers, however they were heard.
questions.pre_read: Does the audit need this detail? If not, what does the privacy policy say about recording it, and who else is entitled to hear it?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 5.1 Use of Information makes policy and law govern how auditors use what they learn, Standard 5.2 requires respect for privacy, and Principle 5 covers what is said in meetings as well as records. The policy limits health data to tasks that need it, and this audit does not. Standard 14.6 asks for documentation of what is relevant to results, so recording it, the runner-up, overreaches.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: workpapers must hold what supports the results so others could redo the work. A colleague's treatment supports nothing here, and the policy bars recording it without need.
wrong_explanations.C: Restricted access suits personal data the work needs. Here the policy bars recording the detail at all, so protecting a record that should not exist misses the rule.
wrong_explanations.D: Human resources handles staff health, but no task of theirs needs this detail and Uwase has no legal or professional duty to pass it on; Standard 5.2 bars the disclosure.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the policy bars recording the detail, so restricting access to the record does not help, and D, because passing it to human resources is an unauthorized disclosure.
Final two: B beats A because documentation covers what is relevant to the engagement's results; a detail the audit does not need stays out, as the privacy policy requires.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, complete documentation means complete for the work, not a record of everything heard; personal data the work does not need is left out when privacy rules say so.

questions.subtopic: 4A1 The mandate and who sets it. Oversight once internal audit is outsourced
questions.question: A Montenegrin charity outsources internal audit to a firm whose partner, Milica, acts as chief audit executive; a trustee wants the audit committee to leave oversight to the firm. Which reply by Milica is BEST?

options.A: Yes: the chief audit executive answers for the function's conformance
options.B: No: the audit committee also approves each engagement's scope
options.C: Yes: the firm's own quality reviews already oversee its work
options.D: No: the audit committee's oversight continues under the contract

questions.key_concept: Outsourcing moves the work, not the board's role: the board still supports and oversees the function, while the chief audit executive answers for conformance.
questions.pre_read: The Standards apply whether internal auditors are employees or a contracted firm. What changes for the board when the whole function is outsourced?
questions.correct_explanation: Domain III says the Standards apply whether internal auditors are employed, contracted or both, and that in every case backing and overseeing the function remains the board's role. The IIA's 2026 Three Lines statement adds that outsourcing leaves the board's accountability unchanged. Milica's own duty for conformance, the closest choice, is real, but it sits beside the board's oversight and does not replace it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a chief audit executive supplied by a firm still answers for conformance. That duty sits beside the board's oversight of the function; it does not take its place.
wrong_explanations.B: The chief audit executive approves each engagement's objectives and scope. The board approves the charter, plan, budget and resource plan, not engagement scopes.
wrong_explanations.C: The firm's quality reviews support conformance, which the chief audit executive answers for. Oversight of the function is the board's, whoever supplies the staff.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the chief audit executive, not the board, approves engagement scopes, and C, because the firm's quality reviews support conformance but never replace the board's oversight.
Final two: D beats A because the chief audit executive's duty for conformance is real but sits beside the board's duty to support and oversee the function, which outsourcing leaves in place.
Exam cue: a contract can change who does internal audit work and who reviews its quality, but the board's oversight of the function stays exactly where it was.

questions.subtopic: 4A1 The mandate and who sets it. Which of two governing bodies is the board
questions.question: A Costa Rican state port's ministry council appoints its directors; its founding law gives the directors alone approval of internal audit's charter. Which body should chief audit executive Valeria BEST treat as the board?

options.A: The directors, as the body able to give internal audit its mandate
options.B: The ministry council, as it appoints the directors who approve the charter
options.C: Both bodies jointly, as each acts as a board over the port
options.D: The executive committee, as the group that runs the port each day

questions.key_concept: Where more than one body governs, the board for internal audit is the body authorized to give it its authority, role and responsibilities.
questions.pre_read: The glossary starts from the highest body charged with governance. What decides which body counts when an organization has two?
questions.correct_explanation: The Standards' glossary deals with organizations that have more than one governing body: for internal audit, the board is whichever body is empowered to give the function its authority, role and responsibilities. The founding law gives charter approval, and with it the mandate, to the directors alone, so they are Valeria's board. The ministry council, the closest choice, appoints the directors, but that does not make it the body that authorizes internal audit.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: appointing the directors gives the council power over them, but with several governing bodies the board is the one empowered to give internal audit its mandate: the directors.
wrong_explanations.C: Two bodies share the board's role only if both are empowered over internal audit. Here the law gives charter approval to the directors alone.
wrong_explanations.D: Reading the board as the people who run the organization fits only where no governing body exists. This port has one empowered over internal audit.

tips: Eliminate: C, because only an empowered body counts and the law empowers the directors alone, and D, because management stands in for the board only where no governing body exists.
Final two: A beats B because, with two governing bodies, the board is the one empowered to give internal audit its mandate; appointing the directors does not make the council that body.

Exam cue: when an organization has layers of governing bodies, ask which one is empowered to give internal audit its authority, role and responsibilities, usually by approving the charter. That body is the board.

questions.subtopic: 4A1 The mandate and who sets it. A refused essential condition the chief audit executive cannot accept
questions.question: A Swiss watchmaker's audit committee refuses yearly talks on whether internal audit's resources suffice; chief audit executive Luca showed examples of the harm, offered alternatives and rejects its reasons. What is Luca's BEST next step?

options.A: Show the committee, with examples, how the missing talks will hurt
options.B: Record the committee's reasons and the conditions that compensate
options.C: Document the committee's reasons and share them, assessor included
options.D: Accept the refusal, as the Standards place no requirement on boards

questions.key_concept: If the chief audit executive rejects why the board refuses an essential condition, the reasons should be recorded, shared and kept for the external assessor.
questions.pre_read: Domain III sets out what happens when the board will not provide an essential condition. Which step fits once examples and alternatives have failed?
questions.correct_explanation: Domain III's introduction sets a path for a refused essential condition, such as Standard 8.2's yearly talk on resource sufficiency. Luca has done the must, showing examples of the harm, and the should, offering alternatives. As Luca rejects the committee's reasons, those reasons should now be written down, shared with the board and senior management, and kept for the external assessor. Recording an agreed substitute, the closest choice, needs an agreement that does not exist.

wrong_explanations.A: Showing the harm with examples is the must, and Luca has already done it. Repeating it adds nothing once the committee has heard and rejected the case.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: reasons plus compensating conditions must be documented when everyone agrees a condition is unnecessary. Luca rejects the committee's reasons, so that branch does not apply.
wrong_explanations.D: The Standards do bind internal auditors, not boards, but that does not end Luca's part: the disagreement should still be written down, shared and kept for the external assessor.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the examples have already been shown and rejected, and D, because a board's freedom from requirements does not end the chief audit executive's part in documenting the disagreement.
Final two: C beats B because documenting reasons with a substitute fits only when everyone agrees the condition is unnecessary; Luca disagrees, so the disagreement itself is recorded and shared.
Exam cue: for a refused essential condition, follow the stage: show the harm with examples, offer alternatives, then document either the agreed substitute or the unresolved disagreement.

questions.subtopic: 4A2 Threats to internal audit independence. A subsidiary head barred from local management
questions.question: A South Korean shipbuilder's group chief audit executive, Min-jun, bars the head of internal audit at its Vietnamese subsidiary from discussing any finding with that subsidiary's chief executive, citing independence. Which assessment is MOST accurate?

options.A: Sound: routing results through the group keeps the subsidiary unit independent
options.B: Unsound: subsidiary heads should be able to speak with local management directly
options.C: Unsound: the subsidiary head should report functionally to that chief executive
options.D: Sound: the group chief audit executive decides who receives results

questions.key_concept: Independence is not isolation: heads of internal audit in subsidiaries or divisions should be able to talk directly with the senior management of their units.
questions.pre_read: A group function protects its independence through its line to the board. Does that mean keeping subsidiary management at arm's length?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 7.1's considerations expect heads of internal audit in subsidiaries, branches and divisions to be able to speak directly with the senior managers of those units, and Standard 13.1 requires internal auditors to communicate with management throughout an engagement. Min-jun may decide who receives final communications, but independence comes from the line to the board, not from silence. Routing everything through the group, the closest choice, mistakes isolation for independence.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: independence rests on the functional line to the board and freedom from interference. Barring talks with local management adds isolation, not independence.
wrong_explanations.C: The functional line runs to the board, not to a chief executive. Direct talks with the subsidiary's management concern communication, not where the head reports.
wrong_explanations.D: Min-jun does decide who receives final communications, but that does not stretch to barring all talks with local management, which Standard 13.1 and the considerations expect.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the functional line runs to the board, never to a chief executive, and D, because deciding who receives final communications does not extend to barring all talks with management.
Final two: B beats A because independence comes from the reporting line and freedom from interference; the considerations want subsidiary heads able to speak directly with their units' managers.
Exam cue: independence is a matter of position and freedom from interference, never of silence. An option that cuts internal audit off from management in the name of independence is usually wrong.

questions.subtopic: 4A2 Threats to internal audit independence. Filling a vacant chief audit executive post
questions.question: A Salvadoran coffee exporter's chief audit executive resigns without notice, and the chief financial officer, the administrative line, offers to run internal audit until a successor starts. Which arrangement is BEST?

options.A: The board itself names who leads internal audit in the meantime
options.B: The chief financial officer leads it, reporting to the board meanwhile
options.C: The most senior internal auditor takes over until a successor starts
options.D: Senior management names an acting head and informs the board

questions.key_concept: If the chief audit executive post falls vacant, the board should appoint one or more interim people; management does not fill it.
questions.pre_read: The board authorizes the chief audit executive's appointment. Does that change when the post is suddenly empty?
questions.correct_explanation: Domain III's introduction says that when the chief audit executive post is empty for any reason, the board should choose who acts until it is filled, matching its essential condition in Standard 7.1 to authorize appointment and removal. Promoting the senior auditor by seniority alone, the closest choice, skips the board's decision; a chief financial officer in charge would put management over the work that assures it.

wrong_explanations.B: A line to the board does not cure it: the board names the interim, and a chief financial officer in charge puts management over work that assures its areas.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a senior internal auditor may well be the right interim choice, but the board makes it. Seniority does not hand over the role by itself.
wrong_explanations.D: Senior management gives input on appointing the chief audit executive; the board authorizes it. An acting head chosen by management and reported later reverses that order.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a line to the board does not stop a chief financial officer in charge from directing assurance over finance, and D, because senior management gives input while the board authorizes the appointment.
Final two: A beats C because the right interim head may be the senior auditor, but the board names whoever acts; the role does not pass by seniority alone.
Exam cue: a vacancy does not move the board's powers. Whoever would appoint or remove the chief audit executive also decides who stands in meanwhile.

questions.subtopic: 4A3 Internal audit and the Three Lines Model. Who defines roles across the lines
questions.question: An Azerbaijani bank's audit committee wants chief audit executive Leyla, as integrator of assurance, to set the roles of risk, compliance and internal audit. Under current Three Lines guidance, who should MOST appropriately set them?

options.A: The board and Leyla, as internal audit integrates assurance
options.B: Senior management alone, as it designs the organization's structures
options.C: Each function's head, for the work that function performs
options.D: The board and senior management, above the three functions

questions.key_concept: The board and senior management define roles. Internal audit coordinates assurance but does not allocate roles, and its own mandate comes from the board.
questions.pre_read: The 2026 Three Lines statement calls internal audit an integrator of assurance. Does integrating mean deciding who does what?
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's 2026 Three Lines statement has the board and senior management set accountability by deciding who is responsible for what, and casts internal audit as an integrator that coordinates assurance without owning second-line work. Senior management alone, the closest choice, does design the structures, but internal audit's role comes from its mandate, which the board establishes under Principle 6. Leyla may advise; the decision is theirs.

wrong_explanations.A: Internal audit coordinates assurance providers and may advise on roles, but deciding roles, its own included, is not its job. Setting them would undermine its independence.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: senior management designs structures and creates second-line roles, but internal audit's role comes from the mandate the board establishes, so the board takes part.
wrong_explanations.C: Each head runs the work inside a function, but someone above the functions decides who does what across them. That is the board with senior management.

tips: Eliminate: A, because internal audit coordinates and advises but does not decide roles, its own included, and C, because roles across functions are set above the functions, not by each head.
Final two: D beats B because senior management designs the structures, but internal audit's role comes from a mandate the board establishes, so the two define accountability together.

Exam cue: integrator of assurance means coordinating and reporting a combined view, never assigning other functions' duties. Who does what across the lines is decided by the board and senior management.

questions.subtopic: 4A4 Objectivity impairments of individual auditors. A stake in the result without a former role
questions.question: As a finance analyst two years ago, internal auditor Lena wrote a Swedish insurer's losing business case against outsourcing claims handling; Lena is now assigned assurance on the outsourced service. Which assessment is MOST accurate?

options.A: No impairment, since the case was written over 12 months ago
options.B: A possible impairment, for Lena to disclose to the activity's management
options.C: No impairment, since a supervisor will review Lena's workpapers
options.D: A possible impairment, for Lena to disclose to a designated supervisor

questions.key_concept: Objectivity can be impaired by a stake in an outcome, not only by past responsibility; a possible or perceived impairment is disclosed.
questions.pre_read: What would Lena gain if the outsourced service looked poor, and how might others read Lena's findings? Then ask who must hear about it.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 2.1 Individual Objectivity requires internal auditors to know and manage their possible biases, and Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity counts potential and perceived impairments, not only actual ones. Poor results would vindicate Lena's losing case, and others could read them that way. Standard 2.3 requires disclosure to the chief audit executive or a designated supervisor. The 12-month rule, the runner-up, concerns past responsibility for an activity, which Lena never had.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the 12-month presumption covers assurance on an activity the auditor once ran. Lena never ran claims, and a stake in the result does not simply lapse with time.
wrong_explanations.B: Standard 2.3 has an auditor tell the chief audit executive, or a supervisor that executive designates. Raising it with the activity's management is the executive's call.
wrong_explanations.C: Supervisory review checks the work, but it does not remove Lena's stake in the outcome or how others see it. An impairment that may affect objectivity must be disclosed.

tips: Eliminate: B, because in assurance work the auditor tells the chief audit executive or a designated supervisor, not the activity's management, and C, because review does not remove a stake in the outcome.
Final two: D beats A because any situation that may sway judgment can impair objectivity; the 12-month presumption covers former responsibility for an activity, which Lena never held.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, ask whether the auditor has a stake in how the results look, not only whether they once ran the activity; a possible impairment is disclosed.

questions.subtopic: 4A5 Confidentiality and proper use of information. A legal duty that covers part of a request
questions.question: Counsel confirms a regulator's notice lawfully requires a Peruvian fishmeal maker's emission-testing workpapers; the inspector also wants overtime workpapers, which no law or policy authorizes releasing. What is chief audit executive Rosa's BEST response?

options.A: Release both sets, since the inspector holds lawful authority
options.B: Release neither until the board approves an outside release
options.C: Release the emission workpapers, and decline the overtime request
options.D: Release both sets, with staff names removed from the overtime set

questions.key_concept: A legal duty permits disclosing confidential information only as far as the duty reaches; anything beyond it stays with authorized parties.
questions.pre_read: Note what counsel confirmed and what the stem says about any authority to release the workpapers.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 5.2 Protection of Information bars giving confidential information to unauthorized parties unless a legal or professional responsibility requires it, and Standard 1.3 Legal and Ethical Behavior requires the disclosures the law demands. Counsel confirms the notice reaches the emission workpapers, so those go. No law or policy authorizes releasing the overtime workpapers, so the inspector is an unauthorized party for them. Removing names, the runner-up, still discloses work no duty or authorization covers.

wrong_explanations.A: Authority to demand some records is not authority to receive all. The notice covers the emission workpapers; nothing requires or authorizes releasing the overtime set.
wrong_explanations.B: A lawful notice is a legal duty to disclose, and Standard 1.3 requires meeting it. Internal approval routes cannot hold back what the law requires.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: removing names suits a disclosure that is owed but must protect privacy. No duty or authorization covers the overtime workpapers, and redaction does not supply one.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the notice sets how far the legal duty reaches, and B, because the owed release cannot hinge on the board's approval; internal review may come first but cannot block it.

Final two: C beats D because confidential information goes outside only to an authorized party or under a legal duty; redaction protects people in an owed disclosure but does not authorize an unowed one.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, a legal duty to disclose opens the door only as wide as the duty; anything beyond it needs its own authorization, or it stays confidential.

questions.subtopic: 4A4 Objectivity impairments of individual auditors. Judging one's own earlier audit conclusion
questions.question: Internal auditor Ana rated a Vietnamese hotel group's payroll controls effective last year; a fraud spanning that year has surfaced, and Ana is assigned to assess how it evaded them. Which assessment is MOST accurate?

options.A: Objectivity intact: running payroll was not Ana's responsibility
options.B: Objectivity intact: Ana's knowledge of those controls speeds the review
options.C: Objectivity at risk: the fraud suggests Ana's earlier work lacked care
options.D: Objectivity at risk: the review would judge the rating that Ana gave

questions.key_concept: The risk of self-review bias arises whenever auditors would judge their own earlier work, an audit conclusion included, not only an activity they once ran.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the engagement would have to evaluate, then test each option's reason against the facts, not only its conclusion.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 2.1 Individual Objectivity names self-review bias, the weaker critical eye people bring to their own work, and Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity counts impairments in appearance as well as in fact. Explaining how the fraud passed controls Ana rated effective means judging Ana's own rating, so objectivity is impaired at least in appearance and Ana discloses it under Standard 2.3. Never having run payroll, the runner-up, settles only the former-responsibility rule.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the refrain rule and the 12-month presumption concern running an activity, but self-review bias also covers judging one's own past audit work, as here.
wrong_explanations.B: Familiarity with one's own earlier view makes a fresh look harder, not easier. Knowing an area best is the warning sign when that earlier view is under review.
wrong_explanations.C: Due care is not infallibility, and controls give only reasonable assurance, so a later fraud alone does not mean poor work. The risk is Ana's stake in the rating.

tips: Eliminate: B, because familiarity with one's own earlier view weakens a critical review rather than helping it, and C, because a fraud found later does not prove the earlier work lacked due care.
Final two: D beats A because self-review bias covers judging one's own past work, an audit rating included; the refrain rule on former responsibility does not set its limit.

Exam cue: on CIA questions, ask whose work the engagement would judge; if it is the assigned auditor's own conclusion, objectivity is impaired at least in appearance, though they never ran the activity.

questions.subtopic: 4A5 Confidentiality and proper use of information. Access left over from a closed engagement
questions.question: Internal auditor Andre still holds the HR system access granted for a Belizean bank's payroll engagement, now closed; follow-up will use evidence management sends. Which view of that access is MOST accurate?

options.A: It should go now: access ends when the work needing it ends
options.B: It should stay: the charter grants internal audit unrestricted access
options.C: It should go at the chief audit executive's next periodic access review
options.D: It should stay until follow-up closes, then be removed

questions.key_concept: Access to information is granted for the work; once the work no longer needs it, the access should be removed and requested again later.
questions.pre_read: List the work still ahead and what each step will rely on before judging the access.
questions.correct_explanation: Principle 5 Maintain Confidentiality keeps information for professional purposes, and Standard 5.2 Protection of Information requires managing the risk of accidental exposure, naming access and copies no longer needed among the function's concerns. Its considerations add that permissions should be revoked once the work no longer needs them. Keeping it until follow-up closes, the runner-up, overlooks that follow-up uses management's evidence, so no remaining work needs the access.

wrong_explanations.B: Unrestricted access lets internal auditors reach what their work needs. It does not mean standing access to personal data after the work is done.
wrong_explanations.C: The chief audit executive's periodic review of access needs is a backstop. Andre already knows the need has ended, and holding the access until then only adds exposure.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: access may stay while work still needs it, but this follow-up uses evidence management sends. Nothing needs the access now, so holding it only adds exposure.

tips: Eliminate: B, because unrestricted access covers what the work needs, not standing access afterward, and C, because the periodic access review is a backstop, not a reason to hold access no work needs.
Final two: A beats D because the follow-up relies on management's evidence, so no remaining work needs the access; it should be removed now and requested again if needed.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, access follows the work: granted when needed, removed when the need ends, and requested again for the next engagement.

questions.subtopic: 4A4 Objectivity impairments of individual auditors. A short acting role in the activity
questions.question: Five months ago internal auditor Chikondi spent three weeks as a Malawian tea estate's acting dispatch manager, on an approved rotation. Which view of Chikondi giving assurance on dispatch's past year is MOST accurate?

options.A: Not presumed impaired: three weeks of cover is too brief to count
options.B: Not presumed impaired: the chief audit executive approved the rotation
options.C: Presumed impaired for the weeks Chikondi was in charge, not the rest
options.D: Presumed impaired: covering as manager counts as holding responsibility

questions.key_concept: Any responsibility for an activity within the previous 12 months, however brief or approved, makes objectivity presumed impaired for assurance on that activity.
questions.pre_read: Did Chikondi hold responsibility for dispatch, and when? Then ask whether the length of the role or its approval changes the rule.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity bars assessing an activity one was responsible for and presumes impairment for assurance when that responsibility fell within the previous 12 months. Acting as dispatch manager was responsibility for dispatch, five months ago. The rule sets no minimum length, so a short spell, the runner-up's ground, still counts, and the presumption covers the activity under review, not only the weeks Chikondi ran it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the Standards set no minimum period. Three weeks in charge of dispatch is responsibility for it, and five months ago is inside the 12 months.
wrong_explanations.B: Approving a rotation decides who covers the role, not whether objectivity is impaired. Standard 2.2's presumption follows the responsibility held, whoever approved it.
wrong_explanations.C: The presumption attaches to the activity Chikondi was responsible for. Testing only the other weeks would still have Chikondi judging a process, staff and decisions Chikondi ran.

tips: Eliminate: B, because approving a rotation does not cure the impairment it creates, and C, because the presumption covers the activity under review, not only the weeks Chikondi was in charge.
Final two: D beats A because Standard 2.2 counts any responsibility within the previous 12 months; the rule has no minimum length of service.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, acting, temporary or rotational roles are still responsibility; test the activity and the 12 months, not how long or how officially the role was held.

questions.subtopic: 4A1 The mandate and who sets it. Direction from an official outside the oversight line
questions.question: A council member of a Brazilian city, outside the audit committee that oversees internal audit, tells chief audit executive Renata to audit a contract a rival council member approved. What should Renata do FIRST?

options.A: Start a short preliminary review to judge whether an audit is warranted
options.B: Consult the audit committee and senior management before acting on it
options.C: Add it to the plan, as elected officials speak for the public
options.D: Decline it, and note it in the audit committee's yearly confirmation

questions.key_concept: Public sector: before acting on an elected official without oversight of internal audit, the chief audit executive should consult the board and senior management.
questions.pre_read: Public-sector internal auditors hear from many elected officials. Who may direct the function's work, and what happens to a request from anyone else?
questions.correct_explanation: The Standards' public-sector section says a chief audit executive should hold back from an elected official's instructions until the bodies overseeing internal audit, the board and senior management, have been consulted; an official with an oversight role is the exception. This council member has none, and Standard 9.4 leaves the plan and significant changes to it for the board to approve. A preliminary review, the closest choice, already acts before that consultation.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: judging whether work is warranted is sound planning, but starting it here acts on an outside official's direction before the bodies that oversee internal audit are consulted.
wrong_explanations.C: Public input may inform the plan, but an official with no oversight role cannot direct it; the board approves the plan and significant changes to it.
wrong_explanations.D: Declining at once settles the request alone, before the consultation the public-sector section expects. Whether the episode belongs in the yearly independence confirmation is a later judgment.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the board, not any official, approves significant changes to the plan, and D, because declining at once skips the consultation that should come first.
Final two: B beats A because even a preliminary review acts on the direction; with an official outside the oversight line, the board and senior management are consulted first.
Exam cue: when an elected official with no oversight of internal audit tries to direct its work, the chief audit executive should consult the board and senior management before acting.

questions.subtopic: 4A2 Threats to internal audit independence. A scope limitation the board leaves standing
questions.question: A warehouse head withheld records from internal auditor Rosa's assurance engagement on a Kenyan brewer's four spare-parts warehouses; talks failed, and the board declined to intervene. How should Rosa's final communication BEST treat that warehouse?

options.A: Omit the warehouse, since the narrower scope is now settled
options.B: Hold the results and elevate the refusal to the board once more
options.C: Conclude on the warehouses examined; the board's minutes hold the reason
options.D: Explain the limitation, and conclude on the warehouses examined

questions.key_concept: An unresolved scope limitation is explained in the assurance final communication itself, and the conclusion covers only the work that could be done.
questions.pre_read: Once the board has heard of a scope limitation and chosen not to act, what does the limitation still change in the engagement's results?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.3 sends an unresolved scope limitation to the board, and the board's choice does not end Standard 15.1's requirement that the assurance final communication explain it to its readers. Standard 14.1 needs sufficient evidence for a conclusion, so it covers the three warehouses examined, and Rosa decides whether the withheld records are themselves a finding. Limiting the conclusion without the explanation, the closest choice, meets only half of that.

wrong_explanations.A: Nothing settled the scope: a board that declines to intervene leaves the limitation standing. Standard 15.1 still has the final communication explain it.
wrong_explanations.B: The board has already heard the matter and declined to act, so escalating again adds nothing. What remains is to issue results that explain the limitation.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the conclusion is rightly limited, but Standard 15.1 puts the explanation of a scope limitation in the final communication itself; board minutes do not reach its readers.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a board that declines to intervene leaves the limitation standing, not settled, and B, because the board has already heard it and the next step is the report.
Final two: D beats C because Standard 15.1 puts the explanation of a scope limitation in the final communication itself; a limited conclusion with the reason left in board minutes is incomplete.
Exam cue: a scope limitation changes results twice: the conclusion covers only what was examined, and the final communication says why. Escalating to the board replaces neither.

questions.subtopic: 4A2 Threats to internal audit independence. Which budget arrangement restricts the work
questions.question: An audit committee member at a Croatian shipyard asks internal auditor Marija which of four budget arrangements could restrict internal audit's work. Which should Marija MOST clearly identify?

options.A: Internal audit's budget sits inside finance's, with its own share tracked
options.B: The board approved less than requested, though enough for the approved plan
options.C: Staff are funded, though not the analytics tool the plan's tests need
options.D: The administrative line reviews the budget before the board approves it

questions.key_concept: A budget is a limit when it cannot fund the planned work, tools included; its location, or a cut that covers the plan, is not.
questions.pre_read: Budget questions tempt you to flag every cut or every link to finance. What actually makes a budget a limit on internal audit's work?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 10.1 has the budget cover what the function needs to deliver its strategy and plan, technology and tools included, and Standard 7.1's considerations call a budget that leaves the function unable to do its work an undue limitation. Funding staff but not a tool the planned tests need does that. A smaller budget than requested, the closest choice, restricts nothing while it still covers the approved plan.

wrong_explanations.A: Standard 10.1's considerations allow for a budget held within a larger one; the chief audit executive should still know the share, track spending and watch its sufficiency, as here.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: receiving less than asked is not itself a restriction. Here the budget still funds the approved plan, while C leaves planned tests without a tool they need.
wrong_explanations.D: Administrative reporting commonly runs budget processes, as Standard 6.2's considerations note; the board still approves the budget, so this review restricts nothing by itself.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a budget may sit inside a larger one if internal audit tracks its share, and D, because administrative review before board approval is a normal budget process.
Final two: C beats B because the test is whether the planned work can be done; a cut that still funds the plan does not restrict it, a missing needed tool does.
Exam cue: judge a budget by whether it lets the function deliver its strategy and plan, tools and training included; where the money sits, or who handles paperwork, is not a limit by itself.

questions.subtopic: 4A2 Threats to internal audit independence. A reporting line set by law
questions.question: By provincial law, a Philippine province's internal audit unit sits in the finance department it audits, and chief audit executive Jose reports to its head. Which safeguard should Jose BEST propose?

options.A: An administrative line to the governor, the functional line staying in finance
options.B: An audit committee of public members, free of management, to oversee it
options.C: A charter amendment moving the unit into the governor's office
options.D: A yearly confirmation of independence from Jose to the finance head

questions.key_concept: Where law places internal audit under managers it audits, an audit committee of public members with no management role can supply the missing oversight.
questions.pre_read: Some public-sector laws fix internal audit low in the structure. When the reporting line cannot be changed, what can still protect independence?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 7.1 builds independence on a direct line to a board, free of the management being audited, and requires Jose to document what in the structure limits it and which safeguards could help. For structures like this, the Standards' public-sector section names one: an audit committee of public members with no management role, overseeing the unit. A line to the governor, the closest choice, still leaves the functional line inside finance.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: reporting administratively to the head of the organization is leading practice, but the functional line would still run to the finance head whose department is audited.
wrong_explanations.C: A board can set reporting lines in a charter where it holds that power, but here a law fixes the placement, and a charter cannot override the law.
wrong_explanations.D: The yearly confirmation of independence goes to the board, not to a manager, and confirming to the audited department's head protects nothing.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a charter cannot override a law that fixes the unit's placement, and D, because the yearly independence confirmation goes to the board, not to the audited manager.
Final two: B beats A because the problem is the functional line, not the administrative one; an independent audit committee gives the oversight that a reporting line to finance cannot.
Exam cue: when a structure fixed by law blocks a direct line to an independent board, look for added independent oversight, documented with the structure's limits, not cosmetic line changes.

questions.subtopic: 4A3 Internal audit and the Three Lines Model. A temporary risk role split at the decision line
questions.question: Until a Mongolian bank without a risk function hires a chief risk officer, its board asks chief audit executive Saraa to keep the risk register and choose responses to top risks. Which course is BEST?

options.A: Decline both, as second-line work would impair independence
options.B: Take on both, with outside assurance until 12 months after hand-back
options.C: Take on the register as advisory work, leaving responses to management
options.D: Run the register only, with outside assurance and a hand-back plan

questions.key_concept: Internal audit may keep a second-line activity for a time, with safeguards. Choosing risk responses stays with management whatever safeguards are offered.
questions.pre_read: Some second-line work can be lent to internal audit with safeguards. Is there any risk task that no safeguard can make acceptable?
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's 2026 statement on enterprise risk management says internal audit must not select or own risk responses, but accepts keeping a risk register as a temporary operating role with safeguards. Standard 7.1 sets those safeguards: an independent third party's assurance during the role and for 12 months after, and a plan to hand it back. Taking on both, the closest choice, stretches safeguards over a decision none can cover.

wrong_explanations.A: Second-line work is not barred outright: Standard 7.1 and the 2026 statement allow a temporary role with safeguards. Only the decision on responses is off limits.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: outside assurance for 12 months after hand-back is the right safeguard for the register, but the 2026 statement bars internal audit from selecting risk responses at all.
wrong_explanations.C: Keeping the register operates a management process, so it is a role beyond internal auditing needing safeguards, not advice. Facilitating a risk workshop would be advisory.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a temporary second-line role is allowed with safeguards, and C, because running the register is operating management's process, which needs safeguards, not an advisory label.
Final two: D beats B because safeguards can cover a temporary register role, but choosing risk responses is a management decision internal audit must not take, safeguards or not.
Exam cue: split a request at the decision line. Internal audit may advise, facilitate or temporarily run support work with safeguards; deciding how to respond to risk always stays with management.

questions.subtopic: 4A1 The mandate and who sets it. Where internal audit's authority comes from
questions.question: A Mexican furniture retailer's new chief executive tells chief audit executive Ximena that internal audit sees records only thanks to the chief executive's yearly memo to staff. Where does that access MOST accurately come from?

options.A: From senior management's support, which the yearly memo spreads
options.B: From its direct line to the board, as recorded in the charter
options.C: From the Standards, which every internal auditor has to follow
options.D: From Ximena's appointment, which the board itself authorized

questions.key_concept: Internal audit's authority, access to records included, comes from its direct line to the board, recorded in the approved charter; senior management promotes it.
questions.pre_read: Several parties help internal audit get access. Which one creates the authority, and which only supports it?
questions.correct_explanation: Internal audit's power to reach records rests on the board: Standard 6.1's considerations say the direct reporting line to the board is what creates the function's authority, and the board approves the charter recording the mandate. Senior management's essential condition there is to back the mandate across the organization and promote that authority. The memo, the closest choice, promotes the authority; it does not create it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: senior management is expected to support the mandate and promote internal audit's authority, and a memo does that. The authority itself is granted through the board.
wrong_explanations.C: The Standards set what internal auditors must do, and so shape the function's responsibilities. They give it no power inside an organization; the board and the charter do.
wrong_explanations.D: The board does authorize the chief audit executive's appointment, but that settles who leads the function. Access comes from the authority the direct line and the charter give it.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the Standards bind internal auditors but grant no power inside an organization, and D, because authorizing the appointment chooses who leads the function; it grants no access.
Final two: B beats A because the board creates the authority through the direct reporting line and the approved charter; senior management supports and promotes it.
Exam cue: separate who grants from who supports. The board grants authority and approves the charter; senior management gives input, then backs the mandate across the organization.

questions.subtopic: 4A2 Threats to internal audit independence. A proposed role beyond internal auditing
questions.question: The chief executive of a Ugandan bank proposes that chief audit executive Okello also lead a new compliance unit; the board has not yet considered it. What is MOST clearly required of Okello?

options.A: Accept, and report the role in the yearly independence confirmation
options.B: Accept once the chief executive agrees to outside assurance over it
options.C: Decline, telling the board and senior management it impairs independence
options.D: Discuss it with the board and senior management, advising on safeguards

questions.key_concept: A proposed role that could impair independence goes to the board and senior management for discussion, with the chief audit executive advising on safeguards.
questions.pre_read: The role is only proposed, and by management. Who must hear about it, and what must the chief audit executive bring to that discussion?
questions.correct_explanation: Under Standard 7.1, a role that could impair independence, whether held now or only proposed, must be talked through with the board and senior management, and the chief audit executive must advise both on safeguards. The board acknowledges the impairment when it approves such a role. Agreeing outside assurance with the chief executive, the closest choice, names a real safeguard but settles the role with management alone, before the board has weighed it.

wrong_explanations.A: The yearly confirmation reports incidents and the safeguards used, after the fact. A proposed role has to be discussed with the board and senior management before it is taken on.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: outside assurance is a real safeguard, but Standard 7.1 has Okello discuss the role with the board and senior management first; the chief executive cannot settle it alone.
wrong_explanations.C: The Standards allow roles beyond internal auditing, such as compliance, with safeguards. Even a role Okello doubts must first be discussed with the board and senior management, not refused alone.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the yearly confirmation reports after the fact, and C, because a compliance role is allowed with safeguards, so a flat refusal skips the required discussion.
Final two: D beats B because the board and senior management must discuss a proposed role and its safeguards; a safeguard agreed with the chief executive alone bypasses the board.
Exam cue: when a role beyond internal auditing is only proposed, the first duty is the discussion with the board and senior management. Safeguards come out of that discussion.

questions.subtopic: 4A3 Internal audit and the Three Lines Model. Owning management's external risk reporting
questions.question: An Indonesian cement maker's finance director asks chief audit executive Dewi to have internal audit write and file its stock exchange risk disclosures. Under The IIA's 2026 risk management statement, which response is BEST?

options.A: Hold it as an ongoing role, with safeguards in the charter
options.B: Hold it for a year, with outside assurance and a hand-back plan
options.C: Leave the disclosures to management, offering advice or assurance on them
options.D: Leave the disclosures to management, as external reports sit outside the charter

questions.key_concept: Under The IIA's 2026 risk management statement, internal audit must not own reporting to external parties; it may advise on or assure that reporting.
questions.pre_read: Some management work can be lent to internal audit with safeguards. Is reporting to outside parties one of those tasks?
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's 2026 enterprise risk management statement says internal audit must not own reporting to external parties, while assurance over risk reporting, and advice on it, are part of its role. Writing and filing the disclosures would be owning them. Charter safeguards, the closest choice, are Standard 7.1's route for roles such as compliance; this task stays with management whatever the safeguards, though Dewi still discusses the request with the board and senior management.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: Standard 7.1's charter safeguards suit roles such as running compliance. The 2026 statement puts owning reporting to external parties among tasks internal audit must not take on.
wrong_explanations.B: The 2026 statement says a temporary assignment may soften the impact, which fits tasks such as keeping a register. Owning reporting to external parties is on its must-not list.
wrong_explanations.D: A charter covering the whole organization can reach external reporting processes, so internal audit may assure them. The disclosures stay with management because of ownership, not charter scope.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a temporary assignment softens only tasks internal audit may hold, not those on the statement's must-not list, and D, because the charter can reach external reporting; ownership is the issue.
Final two: C beats A because charter safeguards fit roles internal audit may hold, such as compliance; The IIA's 2026 statement keeps ownership of external reporting with management.

Exam cue: some tasks no safeguard covers. Under The IIA's 2026 statement, internal audit never owns risk responses, management's follow-up or external reporting; it advises or assures, and discusses the request with the board.

questions.subtopic: 4A2 Threats to internal audit independence. A fee cut to an outsourced internal audit function
questions.question: Mid-year, an Ecuadorian shrimp exporter's finance director cuts the outsourced internal audit firm's hours by a third, leaving the approved plan unmet. Which assessment by Paola, the firm's partner and chief audit executive, is BEST?

options.A: A budget limit to raise now with the board and senior management
options.B: A procurement change for management to settle with the firm
options.C: An impairment to report to the board in the yearly confirmation
options.D: A delivery shortfall for the firm to absorb under its contract

questions.key_concept: An outsourced function's fee is internal audit's budget; a cut leaving the plan unmet is a limitation the chief audit executive reports promptly.
questions.pre_read: The money goes to an outside firm under a supplier contract. Does that make the cut a purchasing matter, or still internal audit's budget?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 10.1 requires the chief audit executive to seek the board's approval of the budget and to tell the board and senior management promptly when financial resources fall short; its considerations add that the board should approve an adequate budget whether the function is insourced or outsourced. A cut that leaves the plan unmet restricts internal audit's work. Calling it procurement, the closest choice, hides a limit on the function from the board.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the firm is a supplier, but the Standards apply to contracted internal auditors too, so its fee is internal audit's budget, which the board approves.
wrong_explanations.C: The yearly confirmation does list incidents that may have impaired independence, but Standard 10.1 requires the impact of insufficient resources to be reported promptly, not months later.
wrong_explanations.D: A firm owes the hours its contract sets, but here the client cut them. The gap is the exporter's internal audit budget falling short, which the board must hear of.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the yearly confirmation comes too late for a shortfall that Standard 10.1 requires reported promptly, and D, because the shortfall comes from the client's cut, not the firm's delivery.
Final two: A beats B because an outsourced firm's fee is internal audit's budget; cutting it limits the board-approved plan, so its impact goes promptly to the board and senior management.
Exam cue: outsourcing changes who does the work, not the rules. Budget approval, and prompt news of any shortfall, still run to the board, whoever supplies the auditors.

questions.subtopic: 4A5 Confidentiality and proper use of information. A fellow assurance provider asks for workpapers
questions.question: A Ugandan insurer's compliance team, an assurance provider internal audit coordinates with, asks engagement supervisor Okello for a claims engagement's workpapers, which hold patients' details, to avoid retesting. Which response is BEST?

options.A: Send them, since coordination calls for sharing work to avoid retesting
options.B: Send a summary of the results, and keep the workpapers back
options.C: Ask the claims manager's consent, as owner of the claims information
options.D: Route the request through the function's release steps for records

questions.key_concept: Releasing engagement records, even to a fellow assurance provider, follows the internal audit function's methodology; a good purpose does not replace the route.
questions.pre_read: The requester is inside the organization and has a sound reason. Does either fact decide whether, and what, Okello releases?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 5.2 Protection of Information bars giving confidential information to anyone not authorized and names the release of engagement records, inside or outside the organization, as a matter for the function; Standard 4.1 requires following the function's methodologies, which Standard 9.3's considerations expect to cover releases. The runner-up is right that coordination avoids retesting, but the chief audit executive runs coordination, and it does not bypass the release route.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: coordination may well end in sharing, but the chief audit executive runs it, and whether records go, and which, follows the function's release route.
wrong_explanations.B: Sharing results is a normal coordination step, but the chief audit executive runs coordination (Standard 9.5) and the release route decides what goes; a summary chosen alone skips both.
wrong_explanations.C: A claims manager's consent does not authorize release of internal audit's records; the function's route decides, applying the privacy rules that cover the patients' details.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a summary is still a release, and choosing it alone skips the route and the chief audit executive's coordination, and C, because a claims manager's consent cannot release internal audit's records.
Final two: D beats A because coordination is the chief audit executive's and explains why sharing may help, while Standards 5.2 and 4.1 leave whether and what to share to the release route.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, a good purpose or a trusted requester never replaces the route for releasing engagement records; apply the methodology, then share what it allows.
